video_title: Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch on Building the Internet for Agents
gist: Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch argues coding agents have flipped Vercel to 60% agent-originated deployments and that the internet is being rebuilt for agent-to-agent traffic, while 80% of tokens on Vercel's gateway now go to open models, commoditizing frontier labs and making agent security the key bottleneck.

insights.claim: Vercel took about 10 years to reach 1 billion deployments and then added another 1.5 billion in roughly the next 10 months, because coding agents now ship the code.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Agent-generated deployment volume is a step-change in infrastructure demand, not incremental growth.
insights.quote: It took us about 10 years to get to a billion deployments.

insights.claim: The share of Vercel deployments originating from coding agents went from 3% at the start of the year to 60% now.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Agent-originated software is becoming the majority of new deployments; platforms agents default to capture the flow.

insights.claim: Vercel positions itself as the universal landing place where all coding agents push code, because code does not do anything until it is deployed somewhere.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Deployment is the chokepoint beneath every coding-agent vendor, so it captures value regardless of which agent wins.

insights.claim: Vercel's open-sourcing of everything for 11 years made it the coding-agent favorite, since models trained on abundant public docs and rules work better with it.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Open documentation becomes a distribution moat when agents choose the tools they know best.

insights.claim: Agents now choose and purchase infrastructure themselves; Vercel sees agents buying services such as Browserbase through its marketplace end to end with no human, using Stripe and Shopify rails.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Agent-as-buyer shifts go-to-market from persuading humans to being the default option agents select.
insights.quote: Agents are now making their choices and they're choosing right.

insights.claim: Reported figures cited in the interview: Vercel at a $9.3B valuation, about $600M annualized revenue, and roughly 485,000 customers; Rauch says customer acquisition is unmatched among infrastructure companies.
insights.speaker: Molly O'Shea (host)
insights.so_what: Gives a scale and valuation anchor for the agent-infra category.

insights.claim: Agent usage drives infrastructure demand vertical because agents write far more code, deploy it, and then browse and consume the internet more than humans ever did; Vercel sees network utilization records daily.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Compute, network and energy demand compound from agents both producing and consuming software.

insights.claim: The web is shifting from machine-to-human to agent-to-agent, so businesses must present agent-optimized interfaces (precise structured information, MCP tools) rather than only pixel-centric human pages.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Companies that do not retool for agents risk being excluded from agent-mediated traffic and commerce.

insights.claim: Bot detection is obsolete when most traffic is bots; what businesses need is bot intelligence on which agents visit and whether they have a good experience.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch (echoing John Collison)
insights.so_what: Analytics and observability for agent traffic is an emerging product category.
insights.quote: What you do need that we provide is bot intelligence.

insights.claim: New agent protocols (MCP for tools, plus machine payment and universal commerce protocols) are the HTML of the agent internet, letting agents transact quickly without browsing human UIs.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Protocol adoption determines which merchants agents can buy from.

insights.claim: Beyond SEO and AEO, publishing content such as transcripts matters because agents search the internet to overcome training cutoffs, so content availability drives agent recall.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Machine-readable content is a distribution channel for media and businesses.

insights.claim: Enterprise software UIs are being displaced by generative interfaces: Vercel staff query a Slack agent that pulls from Salesforce, rendering context-specific views instead of fixed designed screens.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Systems of record persist but the front-end layer shifts to agents, pressuring seat-based SaaS UIs.

insights.claim: Rauch rejects the idea of aggregating lowest-common-denominator SaaS in favor of personalized software, as coding agents make code effectively free and domain-specific tools have far higher enterprise ROI.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Build-versus-buy tilts toward generating bespoke tools on a platform.
insights.quote: I'm a yes code company because I'm now saying coding agents basically make the code free.

insights.claim: Systems of record (customer history, contacts, tickets) remain valuable as critical data infrastructure, but headless: agents pull data out and generate new software on top of it.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Incumbent value migrates to data ownership and API access rather than UI.

insights.claim: Agents trained to run autonomously for long periods pursue goals resourcefully, creating risk of unintended actions and prompt injection hidden in web content that hijacks the agent with the user's tokens and tools.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Guardrails and containment are prerequisites for enterprise agent deployment.
insights.quote: They're like a soldier that has their frontal lobe has been removed

insights.claim: Rauch says the OpenAI-hacking-Hugging Face incident began with an escape from a genuinely good sandbox, and that most organizations have not yet figured out agent security.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Sandbox quality is a differentiator and a large unsolved market.
insights.quote: people have not really figured out agent security yet

insights.claim: Coding agents that are good at writing code are inherently good at hacking because understanding code's rules means understanding how to break them, so enterprises must prioritize defending against AI hackers.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Cyber defense spending should rise with coding-agent capability.

insights.claim: Vercel ran a $1M sandbox bounty; only one researcher with an army of agents made progress, finding a critical Linux vulnerability that Vercel is sharing with industry peers.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Shows AI-assisted vuln discovery is real and reaching foundational infrastructure.

insights.claim: Rauch predicts a rocky next couple of years, a war between good tokens and bad tokens, as AI re-examines insecure human-written legacy code; he opposes banning open models for cyber reasons because the capability is just intelligence.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Defensive token spend and code verification become budget lines; open-model bans are viewed as counterproductive.
insights.quote: a war between four good tokens and four bad tokens

insights.claim: Agents can be used to generate formally verified, near mathematically provable code; Rauch built a proof system to stop AI shipping slop or leaking data, though most world code remains human-written and unverified.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Verification tooling is the likely long-run answer to AI-code risk.

insights.claim: Rauch says he advises 'reject non-understanding': use AI but understand what it does, with the engineer acting like an engineering manager; critical 'capital S' systems demand rigor while vibe coding suits the rest.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Distinguishes demand for rigorous agentic engineering versus casual vibe coding.

insights.claim: Vercel's AI Gateway now sees 80% of tokens going to open models, almost a full flip from the start of the year when traffic mostly went to OpenAI, Gemini and xAI.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Open-model share on a major routing layer suggests proprietary labs face rapid price and share pressure.
insights.quote: 80% of tokens in our network, and this is a tweet that go viral, that went viral, is open models.

insights.claim: Competitive Chinese open models such as Kimi flipped Rauch's view, since open models were previously terrible at coding but now cover most workloads.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Chinese open-weight labs are a credible cost-down force at the frontier's edge.

insights.claim: Enterprises will run a portfolio of models: frontier intelligence for planning, cheap open models for execution, since most tasks do not need maximal intelligence.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Routing between models by task is the default architecture and erodes premium-model share.
insights.quote: I don't need to hire Albert Einstein to solve every problem

insights.claim: Swapping models behind a gateway is one line of code, which gives enterprises negotiating power and makes models modular engines; automatic routing is a promising direction.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Low switching costs imply weak model-provider loyalty and lower margins.

insights.claim: The biggest risk to model labs is retention: users have zero loyalty and the top model rotates every couple of weeks, with new open models appearing 20x cheaper and 98% as good.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Lab valuations rest on retention that is hard to measure and may be fleeting.
insights.quote: the biggest risk is that it's hard for them to understand what their retention is.

insights.claim: Parts of AI usage resemble crypto froth: free promos, subsidized plans, invented token volumes and fake zero-data-retention claims, so 'tourist' usage may inflate reported demand.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Discount reported token volumes and look for non-cheatable retention metrics.

insights.claim: Labs moving into app businesses such as Slack clones signals doubt that the frontier intelligence advantage is enduring, and Vercel's goal is to drive token prices toward zero.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Lab vertical expansion hints at commoditization of tokens.

insights.claim: Rauch says AI lab IPOs are hard because investors cannot forecast like Costco, and free or local models (a small Qwen runs on his MacBook Air) can undercut a lab overnight.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Public-market appetite for lab IPOs may be tempered by unpredictability.

insights.claim: Vercel treats the sandbox, a cloud computer for agents, as a flagship product, arguing quality, reliability and security gaps persist versus neoclouds, with customers migrating off after discount deals.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Agent infrastructure may reward quality and trust over price, a risk for undifferentiated neocloud entrants.

insights.claim: Vercel is pitching a no-lock-in stance across model providers, with zero data retention guaranteed contractually and US-based inference for enterprises.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Neutrality and data guarantees are core enterprise selling points for a gateway layer.

insights.claim: Serverless is not dead but evolving into fluid compute, which scales up with traffic and compresses to nothing, serving functions, sandboxes, sites and agents; Rauch thinks it will define the next decade.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Bursty personal and agent-generated software favors elastic compute.
insights.quote: You need compute that flows like liquid.

insights.claim: Rauch says Vercel's value is iteration velocity rather than speed, and the worst move for companies is to stay put and avoid AI, agents or open models.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Adoption laggards risk being outpaced as the market resets every few weeks.
insights.quote: the primary value that Verscell gives your business is iteration velocity, not speed.

themes.theme: Talent and work in the agent era

insights.claim: Vercel now hires for the ability to direct swarms of agents (agentic engineering) rather than demos, while valuing human communication quality and higher technical competence even in sales roles.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Skill premium shifts toward agent leverage plus human trust-building.

insights.claim: An agent rewrote the migration of Mercedes F1's old web stack onto Vercel in about five minutes, a task that used to take months of consultants, removing a historical sales bottleneck.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Cheap migrations lower switching costs and accelerate enterprise cloud adoption.
insights.quote: the first iteration of the migration of their old stack to the new one actually took five minutes

insights.claim: AI has made work harder, not easier: Silicon Valley CEOs text at midnight and work around 7am-7pm seven days a week, which Rauch finds exciting rather than burdensome.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Intense shipping tempo in the Valley suggests competitive pressure remains high.

insights.claim: Rauch frames the engineer's future role as capital allocator of tokens, echoing Marc Andreessen's 'last job is venture capitalist', while languages like Rust gain because agents absorb human-hostile rigor.
insights.speaker: Guillermo Rauch
insights.so_what: Strict-compiler languages may gain share as agents remove the human learning cost.
